## Transformer Refresher {#sec-ch1}

*From Tokens to the Next-Token Distribution*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- State the decoder-only next-token objective and explain why it is what
  lets a model generate text one piece at a time.
- Trace a single token's vector as it moves through the residual
  stream, the attention sublayer, and the feed-forward sublayer of one
  decoder block.
- Explain causal masking precisely -- which positions a given position
  may and may not attend to -- rather than the imprecise "only the
  previous token" version.
- Distinguish prefill from a single autoregressive decode step, and
  explain concretely what state gets reused between decode steps.

### Why this matters

Every mechanism in the rest of this workbook -- attention variants,
positional schemes, sparsity, mixture-of-experts routing -- is a
modification to the same handful of moving parts introduced here: a
residual stream, an attention sublayer, a feed-forward sublayer, and a
causal mask. If any of those four feel shaky, later chapters will read
as a list of unrelated tricks rather than variations on one theme. This
chapter's job is narrow on purpose: get the shared vocabulary and the
prefill/decode distinction solid, so that "GQA changes how many KV heads
exist" (Chapter 3) or "MoE changes which parameters activate" (Chapter
5) land as small, precise edits to a picture you already have, not new
pictures from scratch.

### Mental model or analogy

Think of the residual stream as a running total printed on a receipt.
Each sublayer in the model doesn't erase what's already printed -- it
adds one more line of adjustment underneath the current total. By the
time the receipt reaches the bottom of the block, the final total
already reflects every earlier adjustment, because each one was added
in, in order.

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy"}
The residual stream is a running total on a receipt. Each sublayer
reads the current total, computes an adjustment, and prints a new line
that *adds* to the total -- it never crosses out or overwrites a
previous line. Where this breaks down: a paper receipt keeps each line
individually readable, so you can always look back and see exactly what
line 3 contributed. The residual stream cannot do that. Every
adjustment is summed into the *same* fixed-width vector, so by the end
you have one number (well, one vector) that reflects every contribution
-- but you cannot read back which sublayer contributed what just by
looking at the final total. That specific limitation is the working
assumption behind why interpretability researchers need extra tools
(activation patching, probing) to recover what an individual sublayer
contributed -- the sum alone doesn't show its work.
:::

### Visual overview

![Tokens become vectors, the same block repeats N times with its own
weights at each repetition, and only the final softmax turns a vector
back into a probability distribution over the vocabulary -- nothing
"decides" the next token before that last step.](figures/rendered/fig-decoder-end-to-end.svg){#fig-end-to-end}

### Technical core

**Tokens and embeddings.** A tokenizer splits text into a sequence of
$S$ discrete tokens, each an integer id into a fixed vocabulary of size
$V$. An embedding table $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{\text{model}}}$
maps each token id to a dense vector of width $d_{\text{model}}$ (the
**hidden dimension**, the width of the residual stream everywhere in
the model). For a batch of $B$ sequences of length $S$, the embedded
input has shape $(B, S, d_{\text{model}})$. We will mostly drop the
batch dimension $B$ below and reason about one sequence at a time --
everything below happens identically and independently across the
batch dimension.

$$
x_i = E[\,\text{token\_id}_i\,], \qquad x_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}
$$ {#eq-embedding}

*In words:* look up a row of a table. That row is where the model's
only "knowledge" of which token this is enters the computation -- from
here on, everything operates on vectors, not token identities.

**The residual stream.** Stack the $S$ embedded vectors into
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{S \times d_{\text{model}}}$. This is the residual
stream at the input to block 1. Every block updates it the same way:

$$
x^{(l+1)} = x^{(l)} + f\big(\text{Norm}(x^{(l)})\big)
$$ {#eq-residual-update}

where $f$ is either the attention sublayer or the feed-forward
sublayer, and $\text{Norm}$ is a normalization step (Chapter 2 covers
exactly which normalization and exactly where it sits; for now, treat
it as "rescale the vector before reading it"). *In words:* a sublayer
never overwrites $x^{(l)}$ -- it reads a normalized copy, computes an
update, and the update is *added back* onto the original,
un-normalized $x^{(l)}$. Shape-wise, $f(\cdot)$ must return something
of shape $(S, d_{\text{model}})$, the same shape it was handed, or the
addition would not type-check. That shape constraint is exactly why
$d_{\text{model}}$ stays constant across every block in a model.

![One block, showing the residual stream as the vertical bar and the
two sublayers branching off it. Notice the stream's width never
changes -- only what gets added to it does.](figures/rendered/fig-decoder-block-anatomy.svg){#fig-block-anatomy width=48%}

**The attention sublayer.** Each block's attention sublayer projects
the normalized stream into three role-specific views:

$$
Q = \tilde{x} W_Q, \quad K = \tilde{x} W_K, \quad V = \tilde{x} W_V
$$ {#eq-qkv}

where $\tilde{x} = \text{Norm}(x)$, and $W_Q, W_K, W_V \in
\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times d_{\text{model}}}$ are learned
weight matrices. $Q, K, V$ each have shape $(S, d_{\text{model}})$.
Rather than using the full width at once, attention splits
$d_{\text{model}}$ into $H_q$ **heads** of width $d_{\text{head}} =
d_{\text{model}} / H_q$, so each of $Q$, $K$, $V$ is reshaped to
$(H_q, S, d_{\text{head}})$ and every head runs the attention computation
below independently, in parallel, on its own $d_{\text{head}}$-wide
slice. *In words:* $Q$ asks "what is this position looking for," $K$
answers "what does this position offer," and $V$ is "what this position
actually contributes if attended to" -- three different linear views of
the same vector, learned separately.

::: {.callout-tip title="Notation note"}
We write $H_q$, not just $H$, for the number of heads -- specifically
the number of *query* heads. In this chapter every head has its own
matching key/value head, so there is no need yet to distinguish a
separate key/value head count. Chapter 3 introduces designs (grouped-
query and multi-query attention) where the query head count and the
key/value head count are genuinely different numbers, at which point
the "q" in $H_q$ starts pulling its weight notationally.
:::

For one head, scaled dot-product attention is:

$$
\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}} + M\right) V
$$ {#eq-attention}

$QK^\top$ has shape $(S, S)$ -- one raw compatibility score per
query/key pair. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}$ keeps those scores
from growing too large as $d_{\text{head}}$ grows (large scores would
push softmax toward a near-one-hot output before the model has learned
anything useful). $M$ is the **causal mask**, and it is the entire
reason a decoder can be trained on whole sequences at once without
cheating:

$$
M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } j \le i \\ -\infty & \text{if } j > i \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-causal-mask}

*In words:* position $i$'s query is allowed to see keys from position
$i$ itself and every position before it ($j \le i$); a key from any
later position ($j > i$) gets an additive $-\infty$, which softmax then
sends to exactly zero weight. This is not "attend only to the previous
token" -- it is "attend to every earlier token, plus yourself, and
nothing later." @fig-causal-mask below makes the difference concrete:
notice that the shape of the allowed region is a solid triangle, not a
single diagonal line.

![Causal visibility for the chapter's running example: the allowed
region (blue) is everything at or before a row's own position, not a
single step back -- position 5 ("the") can see all 4 prompt tokens plus
itself.](figures/rendered/fig-causal-attention-mask.svg){#fig-causal-mask width=55%}

After softmax, each row of the $(S,S)$ weight matrix sums to 1 and is
used to take a weighted average of $V$'s rows, producing a
$(S, d_{\text{head}})$ output per head. The $H_q$ heads' outputs are
concatenated back to $(S, d_{\text{model}})$ and passed through one
more learned projection $W_O$ before being added back onto the residual
stream, per @eq-residual-update.

**The feed-forward sublayer.** The other sublayer, $f$ in
@eq-residual-update, is a position-wise feed-forward network: a small
two-matrix (or, as Chapter 2 will show, sometimes three-matrix) network
applied independently to every position's vector, with no
cross-position mixing at all -- all the cross-position mixing in a
block happens in the attention sublayer.

**Logits and next-token prediction.** After the last block, the
residual stream at the final position, $x^{(L)}_S \in
\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}$, is projected by an output head $W_{\text{out}} \in
\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}} \times V}$ into a vector of **logits** over
the vocabulary, then turned into a probability distribution:

$$
p(\text{next token} = v) = \text{softmax}(x^{(L)}_S W_{\text{out}})_v
$$ {#eq-next-token}

*In words:* one more linear projection turns "the model's final
understanding of this position" into one raw score per vocabulary
entry, and softmax turns those scores into a valid probability
distribution the model (or a sampling procedure) can pick a token from.
Nothing about this step is special to the *last* position -- every
position produces its own next-token distribution, but only the last
position's distribution is the one used to actually extend the
sequence, since the earlier positions' "next tokens" are already fixed
by the real input.

::: {.callout-tip title="Working approximation"}
This chapter presents one decoder block's attention and feed-forward
sublayers as the complete story. A real model stacks $L$ of these
blocks, each with its own weights, and Chapter 2 will show that the
normalization step glossed over here (`Norm` in @eq-residual-update)
has a specific, consequential form and placement. Treat everything in
this chapter as the shared skeleton that later chapters attach real
components to -- it is correct as far as it goes, but it goes only as
far as "here is the skeleton every modern decoder shares."
:::

### Worked example

We trace a complete, tiny causal decoder over the prompt `"The cat sat
on"` (4 tokens, processed by prefill) followed by one decode step that
generates a 5th token, `"the"`. Every number below is verified
programmatically, not hand-derived -- see the Build and Version Note
for how.

**Toy configuration** (deliberately tiny; a real model's dimensions are
hundreds to thousands of times larger, but the mechanics are identical):
$d_{\text{model}} = 4$, $H_q = 2$ heads of $d_{\text{head}} = 2$ each, one
block. Toy (untrained, hand-picked) embeddings:

| Token | Embedding |
|---|---|
| `The` | $(1, 0, 1, 0)$ |
| `cat` | $(0, 1, 0, 1)$ |
| `sat` | $(1, 1, 0, 0)$ |
| `on` | $(0, 0, 1, 1)$ |
| `the` | $(1, 0, 0, 1)$ |

Before tracing the numbers, the same distinction shown here holds at
any scale: prefill happens once (conceptually), decode steps happen
once per generated token, and each decode step only ever adds one new
position's worth of state.

::: {.callout-tip title="Implementation-dependent detail"}
Conceptually, prefill evaluates the prompt positions together and
constructs their per-layer K/V state, which is the model this chapter
uses throughout. A production serving engine may split a long prompt
into chunks for scheduling or memory reasons -- chunking does not
change the logical distinction this chapter draws between prompt
processing and one-position-at-a-time decoding; it is an engineering
detail about how "together" gets scheduled, not a different mechanism.
:::

![Prefill builds the whole cache from the prompt in one pass; each
decode step afterward reads the entire cache but appends exactly one
new K/V slot to it. This figure is reused as-is from the project's
existing KV-cache demonstration -- the mechanics don't change between
this chapter's introduction of the idea and Chapter 3's deeper
treatment of it.](../../figures/rendered/kv_cache_demo.svg){#fig-prefill-vs-decode}

**Prefill.** All 4 prompt tokens are processed together. After
computing $Q$, $K$, $V$ for all 4 positions and applying the causal
mask, head 0's softmax attention weights are:

| Query position | attends to `The` | `cat` | `sat` | `on` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `The` (pos 1) | 1.000 | -- | -- | -- |
| `cat` (pos 2) | 0.500 | 0.500 | -- | -- |
| `sat` (pos 3) | 0.140 | 0.576 | 0.284 | -- |
| `on` (pos 4) | 0.109 | 0.449 | 0.221 | 0.221 |

Every row sums to 1.0, and every blocked (future) position is correctly
absent, not just small -- @eq-causal-mask sent those entries to
$-\infty$ before the softmax ever ran. Notice `sat` (row 3) puts most of
its weight (0.576) on `cat`, not on itself or on `The`; that specific
number is a direct, checkable consequence of the toy $W_Q$/$W_K$
matrices, not a property of causal masking itself -- causal masking
only decides *which* positions are eligible, never how the weight is
split among them.

Prefill's output for this block includes the full $(4, 4)$ residual
stream after the attention sublayer's update has been added in, but
that residual stream is *not* what gets cached. What actually persists
for reuse is each layer's own $K$ and $V$ projections -- computed from
that layer's input, before the attention sublayer's output is folded
back into the residual stream (Chapter 3 gives this retained state a
name: the KV-cache). The residual stream is recomputed fresh at every
step from whichever tokens are currently being processed; only the
per-layer $K$/$V$ rows persist unchanged across steps. (Some
architectures apply a position-dependent transform to $K$ before it is
cached -- Chapter 3 covers this -- so the cached row is not always
identical to the raw projection shown here, but it is still derived
once per position and reused, never re-derived from the residual
stream.)

**Decode step.** To generate token 5, the model embeds only the new
token `the`, computes *its own* $Q$, $K$, $V$ (a single new row, not a
$(5,4)$ recomputation), and reuses the 4 cached $K$/$V$ rows from
prefill unchanged. Head 0's attention weights for this one new query,
over all 5 now-available keys, are:

| Query position | `The` | `cat` | `sat` | `on` | `the` (self) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `the` (pos 5) | 0.075 | 0.310 | 0.153 | 0.153 | 0.310 |

Two things to check against @eq-causal-mask: this row has *no* blocked
entries, because position 5 is the last position and every other
position is at or before it; and the weights still sum to 1.0 across
all 5 entries. The state reused from prefill (`K`/`V` for positions 1
through 4) is bit-for-bit identical to what prefill produced --
generating token 5 did not touch positions 1 through 4 at all.

### Compare and contrast

| Aspect | Encoder-decoder | Decoder-only |
|---|---|---|
| Objective | An encoder reads the full input bidirectionally; a separate decoder generates output conditioned on it | One stack reads and generates using the same causally-masked self-attention throughout |
| Typical use | Translation, summarization with a distinct source/target | Open-ended text generation, chat, most current general-purpose LLMs |
| Covered in this workbook | Not covered -- named here only for contrast | Every remaining chapter assumes this architecture |

: Encoder-decoder vs. decoder-only: this workbook's scope is decoder-only, stated explicitly rather than left implicit {#tbl-architectures}

### Check your understanding

Full solutions are in [Answer Key: Chapter 1](#sec-solutions-ch1), not below,
so you can attempt these before checking:

1. **Quick check.** What does the residual stream carry from one block to
   the next -- the raw output of the most recent sublayer, or something
   else? ________________________________________________
2. **Explain.** Why does a decoder-only objective let the model
   generate text one token at a time, in a way that a bidirectional
   encoder's objective does not? ________________________________________________
3. **Calculation.** For a toy config with $d_{\text{model}} = 8$, $H_q =
   2$ heads, and $S = 5$: what is $d_{\text{head}}$, and what is the
   shape of the raw attention score matrix $QK^\top$ for one head, before
   masking? ________________________________________________
4. **Misconception check.** True or false, and why: "causal masking
   means each token can only attend to the immediately previous token."
   ________________________________________________
5. **Misconception check.** True or false, and why: "the residual
   stream is a separate memory database the model writes facts into and
   reads back later." ________________________________________________

*(Space intentionally left for written answers if you are using this as
a workbook exercise, not only a reading.)*

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"The Transformer generates the entire response in one forward pass."**
It does not. One forward pass produces exactly one next-token
distribution, for one additional position. A 50-token response requires
at least 50 forward passes (one prefill pass over the prompt, then one
decode step per generated token) -- the model has no mechanism for
"seeing ahead" to token 50 while generating token 2. This misconception
is worth taking seriously because it is exactly backward from how
latency actually behaves in production: generation cost scales with
*response* length, almost independently of how long the *prompt* was
processed in a single prefill pass.
:::

### Applied exercise

Pick a toy config of your own: choose $d_{\text{model}}$, number of
layers $L$, and number of heads $H_q$ (make sure $d_{\text{model}}$ is
divisible by $H_q$). For a single token's forward path through **one**
full block, write down the shape of every intermediate tensor: the
input vector, $Q$/$K$/$V$ before and after splitting into heads, the
per-head attention output, the concatenated output, and the vector
added back onto the residual stream. Check your shapes against
@eq-qkv and @eq-attention -- every shape should be traceable to
$d_{\text{model}}$ and $H_q$ alone. If you want a check with real
numbers instead of just shapes, redo the trace above with your own
$d_{\text{model}}$/$H_q$ and toy embeddings; the same programmatic
verification approach applies.

### Interview lens

A common interview framing is: *"Walk me through what happens
differently between processing a 500-token prompt for the first time
versus generating the 501st token."* A strong answer distinguishes
prefill (conceptually, all 500 positions evaluated together, building
per-layer K/V state for the whole prompt -- possibly split into chunks
by the serving engine, which doesn't change the logical picture) from a
decode step (one new position, reusing the 500 cached K/V rows
unchanged, only computing K/V for the new token) -- and explicitly
rejects "the model re-reads the whole prompt every time," which is the
same misconception as this chapter's headline one, just phrased in
systems terms. See workbook 02 (ML Interview Practice) for more on how
to structure this kind of answer under time pressure.

### Chapter recap

- A decoder-only model conditions strictly on earlier positions; nothing
  about its objective lets it "see ahead."
- The residual stream is additive and constant-width: sublayers add
  updates to it, they never replace it or change its dimensionality.
- Attention has three roles ($Q$, $K$, $V$), a causal mask that allows
  every earlier-or-equal position (not just the immediately previous
  one), and a softmax that turns raw scores into a weighted average.
- Prefill conceptually evaluates the whole prompt together and produces
  cached per-layer K/V state (the residual stream itself is not that
  cached state); each decode step reuses that cached state and adds
  exactly one new position's worth of new state.
- Generating $N$ tokens costs at least $N$ forward passes -- there is no
  single-pass shortcut.
